lesson.title: Why Randomize: Letting Chance Do the Balancing
lesson.summary: Randomization assigns subjects to treatment groups by chance so that, on average, the groups are similar in every way except the treatment, controlling for both known and unknown confounding variables.
lesson.body:
Suppose researchers want to know whether a new tutoring program raises test scores. If they let students choose whether to join the program, motivated, well-supported students would likely sign up more often than struggling or disengaged ones. Any later difference in test scores could then be explained by the tutoring program, by the underlying motivation of who joined, or by some mix of both. Motivation here is a confounding variable, a factor that is tangled up with the treatment in a way that makes it impossible to tell which one is actually driving the outcome. Randomization exists to prevent exactly this problem.

When subjects are assigned to treatment groups purely by chance, such as by flipping a coin or drawing names, no personal trait, motivation, prior ability, age, health status, or anything else, gets to influence which group a subject lands in. Across many subjects, chance tends to spread every such trait roughly evenly between groups, not perfectly for any single characteristic, but without any systematic favoritism. This is what statisticians mean when they say randomization balances the groups: it does not guarantee identical groups, but it removes any predictable direction of imbalance, which is precisely how bias is defined, a systematic tendency to be wrong in one direction.

The deepest advantage of randomization is that it handles confounding variables researchers have not even thought to measure. A researcher who suspects motivation matters could try to match tutoring and non-tutoring students by motivation score, but that only controls for the confounders that were anticipated. Randomization protects against unanticipated confounders too, family income, sleep habits, learning style, because none of these traits gets a vote in the coin flip. This is why randomized experiments can support cause-and-effect conclusions in a way that observational studies generally cannot: if the groups were formed by chance and end up with different outcomes, chance is a poor explanation for a sizable, consistent difference, leaving the treatment as the most credible remaining explanation.

Return to the tutoring example as a worked hypothetical. A school has 120 eligible ninth graders. Researchers write each student's name on a slip, mix the slips thoroughly, and draw 60 names for the tutoring group, leaving the remaining 60 as the control group. By design, highly motivated students and less motivated students each have the same chance of being drawn into either group, so the two groups should end up with roughly similar mixes of motivation, prior GPA, and every other trait, measured or not. If the tutoring group's test scores rise substantially more than the control group's, motivation is no longer a plausible rival explanation, because it was not allowed to sort itself unevenly between the groups in the first place.

Randomization does not remove every threat to a good experiment. It does not, by itself, prevent placebo effects or evaluator bias, which is why blinding remains a separate and complementary safeguard, and it does not guarantee that groups are identical in small samples, where chance imbalances can still occur. What randomization reliably delivers is the removal of systematic bias in how groups are formed, replacing a researcher's or a subject's judgment, and all the confounding that judgment invites, with the impartiality of chance.
